content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a two-stage segmentation system for somas in volume EM data. The system consists of a localization network, and a per-instance segmentation network. It is tested with a Unet and Swin-UNETR backbone, and applied on the Full Adult Fly Brain dataset. Soma basic statistics about the soma distribution in the fly brain are derived from the segmentation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The main strength of the paper is the contribution of manually created ground truth annotations for 204 somas. 
The main weakness is the limited novelty in terms of ML methods. The paper just uses standard techniques to solve a very specific problem, which to a large degree is implicitly already addressed by volume EM segmentation methods.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is generally clearly written, but has some confusing statements about existing EM data (see below). The paper does not introduce any machine learning innovations -- the networks used are standard 3d architectures, as is the two-stage localize-segment approach to instance segmentation. The techniques used to deploy the proposed method over a large dataset are standard for the field of volume EM data analysis. In evaluations, the authors show that their approach compares favorably to their own custom baselines, as well as methods adapted from nuclei segmentation. The evaluation would be strengthened, if they also compared their full volume results to existing public segmentations of the FAFB dataset, particularly in terms of cell identity, which would not require separating the somas from their neurites in the fine-grained segmentations.

Questions:
- The soma is continuous with the neurites that emanate from it. In the context of your work, how do you define where the soma ends and the neurite begin, and how does that impact the metrics you report?
- You mentioned using self-training. How important was it to get your results? How much additional data did it generate?
- Some "somas located at the boundary of the blocks" are reported to be omitted because they "are hard to annotate". However blocks appear to be a side effect of how you subdivided the data -- the somas you omit are presumably not hard to annotate in the complete dataset. If so, why exclude them from the metrics?
- Why is it necessary/helpful to have the 2px wide soma boundary layer?
- What happens when the predicted segments for two or more seeds overlap?
- "Through this operation, the eroded annotations of somas are labeled as instance seeds, which provides location information for each annotated soma". Does this include the use of a connected components algorithm, and does it mean the annotations are at the semantic level only (no instances)? If so, why not create instance data directly?
- The movie you uploaded shows discontiguities in soma identity as it scrolls through the z axis. What causes them, and how does that impact the statistics you report?


Comments:
- The text mentions "absence of EM dataset specifically annotated for somas", and that existing reconstructions include whole neurons -- i.e. soma and its branches in a single segment. This is technically correct, however, with a bit of work, the soma could be extracted from these segments, for instance based on their skeleton representation.
- The paper says "existing works cannot directly provide accurate soma distribution and morphology information" and that the "the shape and position of the soma cannot be accurately predicted" with standard EM reconstruction algorithms. This isn't really correct in light of the comment above.
- Fig 1a shows some merged (green) component containing non-soma matter. Could you please comment on what this is?
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, the paper shows that fairly standard instance segmentation approaches can be used to segment somas in volume EM datasets. The paper also contributes a dataset of ~200 manually annotated somas. However, it is unclear what exactly got annotated as soma, and two orders of magnitude more somas are already available as parts of neurons within existing public segmentations of the same dataset.

The statistical analysis is too superficial to yield any biological insights, and is based on a crude subdivision of the brain into optical lobel and central brain parts, which does not take into account any of the visible large-scale structure of the brain. It also lacks comparison to the two publicly existing segmentations of the FAFB dataset (flywire.ai, FAFB-FFN1), or similar statistics extracted from other fly brain samples (https://www.janelia.org/project-team/flyem/hemibrain).

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a dataset and method for localization and segmentation of (biological) neuron cells from very high resolution images collected by Electron Microscopy (EM). A large scale dataset was presented and performance of the proposed method was compared against a few existing methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: Soma reconstruction is a useful step in the overall connectomic reconstruction, and a dataset for this task will assist *some* researchers in  the EM connectomics to improve their methods.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Scope: The scope of this paper is narrow for an ICLR paper. Soma segmentation is one step of the overall connectomic reconstruction, which itself is a niche area of ML/CV application. I am not confident the impact of this work will have (or the attention it will draw) in overall ML community.
In fact, the cellular organization of neurons in fruit fly is significantly different than that of mammals. I dont  know how this work would perform on mammal neurons. 

Technical contribution: There is nothing new that this paper presents that adds to our collective knowledge or understanding of ML/CV. Is there a challenge the method faced that is out of the ordinary? If there are such challenges, how do they relate to (i.e., how do they help solving) problems in any other field other than fruit fly connectomics community?
The paper seems to describe straightforward application of U-Nets (which has been heavily utilized in medical AI since its inception), post/pre-processing, data specific details that only relates of EM connectomics, and system level implementation details.
content.summary_of_the_review:
In my opinion, ICLR is not the appropriate venue for this paper. It may receive more attention if submitted to medical/biological/neuroscience conf or journals. 

Also, I think this paper would be better off focusing either on the dataset or the method. If this is a dataset paper, it should concentrate more on data properties, task descriptions (preferably multiple and how they are important), evaluation etc.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors present a large collection of segmented somas from an EM dataset of the entire fruit fly brain. They also present their algorithm for generating these segmentations in an efficient manner and compare their algorithm against two baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- This was surely a huge undertaking, and the effort to make such a dataset available is to be commended. Segmentation of cells (or in this case, somas) in 3D is notoriously difficult. I have no doubt that the dataset will be of interest to the EM community and those studying the connectome, though I have reservations about how wide of an audience at ICLR will have an interest in this work.
- The evaluations demonstrate thorough consideration of the quality of the results. The comparison with two baseline methods for three different metrics demonstrate the relative effectiveness of their method. The ablation study demonstrates that the size used was optimal. The statistics seem to indicate that there is not a strong bias artifact between different regions, though some additional evaluation could be helpful here (see below).

Weaknesses:
- My primary concern with the work is that it may be too specialized to be of a wide interest for ICLR. The authors have argued that soma reconstruction is crucial for understanding the connectome, but how significant is that advancement to the ICLR community?
- The evaluation using statistics is somewhat weak, other than to confirm that the algorithm does not degenerate in certain regions. Are there other studies that these statistics could be compared against quantitatively to give a more solid justification of the results?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Overall, the paper is well-written, easy to read, and clear. 
- I have some reservation about the novelty of the dataset, as expressed above. I have some doubt about the significance of this dataset to the wider community of ICLR. It would help if the authors did more to argue for this -- perhaps some subsequent analysis that would exemplary of significance of the findings made possible by the dataset.

Suggestions:
- The authors evaluate on three blocks. There is some concern if this is a sufficiently representative dataset since there is likely much diversity in cell shape and morphology between regions (as the authors do note). Could the authors note the regions from which the three blocks were extracted, and argue that this is sufficient?
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors are commended for a significant undertaking in making this dataset available. The paper is well-written and the evaluation well-thought out, though weak in some areas. However, my hesitations about the broad interest in the dataset and what kind of significant biological findings this work can enable prevent me suggesting it be accepted.

content.title: Accurate and Efficient Soma Reconstruction in a Full Adult Fly Brain
content.abstract: Neuron reconstruction in a full adult fly brain from high-resolution electron microscopy (EM) data is regarded as a cornerstone for neuroscientists to explore how neurons inspire intelligence. As the central part of neurons, somas in the full brain indicate the origin of neurogenesis and neural functions. However, due to the absence of EM datasets specifically annotated for somas, existing deep learning-based neuron reconstruction methods cannot directly provide accurate soma distribution and morphology. Moreover, full brain neuron reconstruction remains extremely time-consuming due to the unprecedentedly large size of EM data. In this paper, we develop an efficient soma reconstruction method for obtaining accurate soma distribution and morphology information in a full adult fly brain. To this end, we first make a high-resolution EM dataset with fine-grained 3D manual annotations on somas. Relying on this dataset, we propose an efficient, two-stage deep learning algorithm for predicting accurate locations and boundaries of 3D soma instances. Further, we deploy a parallelized, high-throughput data processing pipeline for executing the above algorithm on the full brain. Finally, we provide quantitative and qualitative results to validate the superiority of the proposed method, as well as comprehensive statistics of the reconstructed somas in the full adult fly brain from the biological perspective.
